clue.text: Cheerful sound when a buzz reaches our editor

parts.note: sound as in healthy or reliable, a sound argument
a hum is a low buzzing noise
taken as written
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A happy noise goes up when a buzzer message gets through to the editor of our paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheerful sound' looks like one phrase, but sound is the first piece of wordplay, meaning healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone good-humoured is in a genial, pleasant mood, a near synonym of cheerful.

clue.text: More impressive piece of kitchen equipment, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the kitchen item is matched by its pronunciation, not its spelling

parts.note: a grater shreds cheese and vegetables

explanation.surface: Someone admires a smarter bit of kitchen kit.
explanation.definitionFit: Greater is the comparative of great, so it means bigger or more impressive.

clue.text: Ransack her soon, but not at sea

indicators.note: to ransack a place is to turn it upside down, so the following letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Pirates are told to loot her cabin quickly, but only once the ship has docked.
explanation.definitionFit: Onshore means on the land rather than out on the water, the opposite of being at sea.

clue.text: Hilary almost promises to be funny

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the name stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: the name as written, before its last letter goes
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: Hilary all but guarantees to be a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: IOU stands for 'I owe you', a signed promise to repay a debt.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hilarious is extremely amusing, a stronger synonym of funny.

clue.text: "King Goldfinger" puts girl's name in manuscript

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside, so the name sits within the abbreviation

parts.note: MS is the usual abbreviation for manuscript
Ida is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A writer slips a girl's name into the manuscript of a Bond-style thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like a Bond title; in Greek myth the king turned everything he touched to gold.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical king whose touch made gold is a literal golden finger, a playful description of him.

clue.text: International warder in prison that is open

parts.note: the United Nations is the international body
screw is slang for a prison officer

explanation.surface: A prison guard from abroad works in a jail that is not locked.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a prison warder is a screw.
explanation.definitionFit: To unscrew a lid or jar is to twist it off, which opens it.

clue.text: Gent won't start on wine, having wind

indicators.note: refusing to start means the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: the word as written, before its first letter goes
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gentleman refuses to begin drinking because he has indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as flatulence; it is the verb, to twist round.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind strands together is to twist or coil them, which is what entwining means.

clue.text: Make a gesture of glee and generate some warmth

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the gleeful gesture of anticipation
second meaning: the friction warms cold palms

explanation.walkthrough: The same action serves both as a sign of gloating pleasure and as a way of warming cold fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbing palms together is both a show of delighted anticipation and a practical way to warm them by friction.

clue.text: Equipment for tile distorted by sun

indicators.note: distorted means bent out of shape, so the letters lose their original order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tiler needs gear because heat from the sun has warped the tiles.
explanation.definitionFit: A utensil is a tool or implement, so the word stands for a piece of equipment.

clue.text: Desmond, old soldier, needing work on computer system

parts.note: Des is the short form of Desmond
KT abbreviates knight, a mounted soldier of old
OP abbreviates opus, a work

explanation.surface: Des, a retired serviceman, has to work at his computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old soldier' suggests a veteran; here it is a knight, abbreviated KT.
explanation.definitionFit: A desktop is a personal computer built to sit on a desk, as opposed to a laptop.

clue.text: Gluttons with ability to rush? It's an impossibility

parts.note: greedy eaters are called pigs
might is power or capability
to fly is to dash or hurry

explanation.surface: Greedy eaters who could also hurry would be a contradiction in terms.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a sarcastic reply meaning something will never happen.

clue.text: Known to doctor holding specs, alfresco

parts.note: a secret that is known is out

indicators.note: something holding another has it inside, so the abbreviation wraps round the pair of round shapes

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
two O shapes look like a pair of spectacles

explanation.surface: An optician's patient eats outside, known to the doctor who holds the glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: Specs are spectacles, pictured as two round letters side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfresco means in the open air, from Italian, so it matches outdoor.

clue.text: I'm working on files, having rings to break

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it apart, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An office worker busy with folders has to break off when the phone rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rings' suggests a phone interrupting the filing; both it and the little word after it are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting files into order is arranging them, a typical clerical job described by the participle.

clue.text: Bird's nest, one held by Jane Rochester

indicators.note: something held by another is gripped inside it, so the numeral goes within the surname

parts.note: the heroine of Charlotte Bronte's novel marries Mr Rochester; her maiden name is the surname needed
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A bird's nest is said to be in the possession of Jane, Mrs Rochester.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Eyre ends with the heroine married to Rochester, so 'Jane Rochester' is Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is the high nest of an eagle or other bird of prey.

clue.text: Crush more than half of what tree?

indicators.note: taking half of a word keeps only its first two letters and drops the rest

parts.note: over means more than, as in over fifty
the word as written, before half of it goes
the elm is a tree

explanation.surface: Someone asks which tree it is that would flatten something more than half its size.
explanation.definitionFit: To overwhelm an opponent is to defeat them completely, much as crushing them does.

clue.text: Unnatural tails seen to be fundamental

indicators.note: something unnatural is not in its normal state, so these letters take an altered order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Odd-looking tails on an animal are spotted and judged to be basic to its nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Essential and fundamental both mean basic, forming the core of something.

clue.text: Conservatories will display recent strains

parts.note: hot means new and fresh, as in hot off the press
a strain is a family line, and so is a royal house

explanation.surface: Glasshouses show off the newest plant varieties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strains' suggests plant breeds, fitting the gardening picture, but here it means lineages, like the House of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: A hothouse is a heated glass building for growing plants, much like a conservatory.

clue.text: Warm garment for best empty tabby

parts.note: top means best, as in top marks
a tabby is a striped cat
O, a zero, stands for nothing, and goes inside

explanation.surface: A coat meant for the finest tabby, whose stomach is empty.
explanation.walkthrough: The empty O sits inside the cat with no signal word for the insertion, a liberty of this clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A topcoat is an overcoat, a heavy outer garment worn for warmth.

clue.text: Bygone actor, one featured in musical

indicators.note: a performer featured in a show appears within it, so the numeral goes inside the title

parts.note: Oliver! is Lionel Bart's musical based on Oliver Twist
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An actor of yesteryear once starred in a stage musical.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurence Olivier was the leading English stage and film actor of the twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Olivier died in 1989, so he is an actor from the past.

clue.text: Reorganise half reel, a dance

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only its first two letters, the rest dropping away

parts.note: the word as written, before half of it goes
a jig is a lively folk dance

explanation.surface: A dance instructor rearranges half a reel into another dance.
explanation.walkthrough: A reel is a Scottish dance, adding to the dancing picture, but only its first half is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To rejig something is to rearrange or reorganise it, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Italian composer does enormous wrong in Rhode Island

indicators.note: in places the preceding letters inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: RI is the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island
OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for very large
a sin is a moral wrong

explanation.surface: An Italian composer commits a huge offence in an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: OS for outsize is a clothing size used in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini was the Italian composer of The Barber of Seville and William Tell.

clue.text: Jeeves — only half there — goes to phone, scoffing

indicators.note: someone only half there is missing a part, so the name keeps just its first half

parts.note: the name of P G Wodehouse's butler, before it is halved
to ring is to phone someone

explanation.surface: Jeeves, the absent-minded butler, answers the phone and sneers at the caller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only half there' paints a dim-witted Jeeves but signals that only half the name is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeering and scoffing both mean mocking someone with derisive remarks.

clue.text: Cloths needed for messy sink and pan

indicators.note: messy means untidy and jumbled, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wiping cloths are called for after the washing-up leaves the sink and pan in a mess.
explanation.definitionFit: Napkins are small squares of cloth used at the table to wipe the mouth and hands.

clue.text: Eyes rest, holding "Good Housekeeping", initially

indicators.note: something holding another wraps round it, so the first word goes outside the letters chosen

parts.note: to sit is to rest

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters, here of each word of the magazine title

parts.note: the first letters of the two words of the magazine title

explanation.surface: Someone rests their eyes by reading a homemaking magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Good Housekeeping is a long-running homes magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Sight is the faculty of seeing, and eyes stands for it by metonymy.

clue.text: Most inquisitive number wants siesta not to end

indicators.note: not to reach its end means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: NO is the abbreviation for number
the word as written, before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: The nosiest person wants an afternoon nap that never ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' tempts towards a numeral; it is the abbreviation No.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosiest is the superlative of nosy, meaning prying or overly curious.

clue.text: Demonstrating how to sing outside

indicators.note: something outside another surrounds it, so the verb goes round the question word

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher shows pupils how to sing in the open air.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing and demonstrating both mean presenting something so others can see it.

clue.text: First witness

definitions.meaning: first meaning: coming at the beginning
second meaning: to sign a document with one's letters as a witness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Witness' reads as a noun, but it is the verb: to put one's initials to a document to attest it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means occurring at the start, and as a verb means to mark a document with one's initials in attestation.

clue.text: Tory with time to be in marketing and writing novels

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit within it, so the party member and time go inside

parts.note: selling is the business of marketing goods
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician takes time out of a sales career to write fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Storytelling is the craft of narrating tales, which is what writing novels involves.
